source.title: (E,E′N) and (E,E′NN) Experiments at NIKHEF, Mainz and JLab and Open Problems in One- and Two-Nucleon Emissions

accepted.question_text: How can the long-standing discrepancy between spectroscopic factors extracted from low-energy exclusive (e,e′p) measurements and spectroscopic factors predicted by nuclear many-body theory be resolved in a reaction framework that consistently includes final-state interactions, current-operator ambiguities, and relativistic effects? In particular, can one explain why low-Q² analyses report strongly quenched valence-shell strengths while higher-Q² analyses give substantially larger values, without attributing the difference to uncontrolled model dependence in the reaction mechanism?

evidence.quote: However, model calculations produce spectroscopic factors Sα much larger than those extracted in low-energy (e,e′p) data.

A possible Q2-dependence of spectroscopic factors, jumping from values around 0.6–0.7 at low Q2 to unity at Q2 ≥ 1 GeV2, simply means that something is not under control in either experiment or theory or both.

A striking feature coming out of the present analysis of (e,e′p) world data is an apparent Q2 dependence of the extracted spectroscopic factors. This is clearly not acceptable and indicates that something is missing in the theoretical treatment of the reaction mechanism.

accepted.question_text: What fully unfactorized treatment of exclusive (e,e′p) reactions can replace model-dependent reduced-cross-section and transparency extractions, while consistently incorporating relativity, final-state interactions, and spin-orbit effects? The unresolved issue is how to compute and compare direct exclusive cross sections across kinematics without relying on factorized formulas whose interpretation changes with the choice of electron-nucleon current, optical potential, or transparency prescription.

evidence.quote: One certainly should measure exclusive cross sections instead of providing (model dependent) reduced cross sections or transparencies. On the theory side a consistent approach is desirable, where relativity and FSI interactions are appropriately taken into account in calculating an unfactorized cross section. In particular, spin-orbit effects should be investigated.
Thus T is a heavily model dependent quantity.

accepted.question_text: How does the normal recoil polarization P_N in exclusive (e,e′p) scattering vary with Q², and can that dependence be used to isolate the energy dependence of final-state interactions well enough to clarify nuclear transparency and, ultimately, color transparency? Because P_N vanishes in the absence of final-state interactions, the open problem is to determine whether systematic polarization measurements can cleanly separate genuine attenuation effects from competing reaction-mechanism uncertainties.

evidence.quote: Without FSI, PN = 0. Therefore PN is a good candidate to look at when studying nuclear transparency, as its Q2 dependence reflects the energy dependence of FSI.

As the normal recoil polarization PN vanishes without FSI, its Q2 dependence in exclusive (e,e′p) reactions deserves a detailed study in connection with the problem of nuclear transparency and, ultimately, of color transparency.

accepted.question_text: Do nucleons bound inside nuclei undergo medium-dependent modifications of their electromagnetic form factors, and if so, how can those modifications be disentangled from conventional nuclear effects such as meson-exchange currents, isobar configurations, and final-state interactions in polarization-transfer observables? A related open direction is whether more precise super-ratio measurements, including analyses beyond 4He and on nuclei such as 16O, can separate genuine in-medium structure changes from reaction-model ambiguities.

evidence.quote: However, it has proven to be a very difficult task to disentangle changes of the nucleon structure from other conventional nuclear effects, such as meson-exchange currents, isobar configurations and FSI, because the nucleon form factors of a bound nucleon are not observable.
A proposal for a similar analysis on 16O is under discussion.
Measuring the components of the induced (transfer) polarization, on the other side, gives important information about possible medium modification of the nucleon electromagnetic form factors.

accepted.question_text: What reaction mechanisms generate the enhanced transverse strength and nearly momentum-independent high-missing-momentum cross section seen in exclusive 16O(e,e′p) measurements at high missing energy, where distorted-wave one-nucleon knockout underpredicts the data and two-nucleon emission channels contribute substantially? More broadly, where exactly does the single-particle picture of one-nucleon knockout break down as missing momentum and missing energy increase?

evidence.quote: There is accumulating evidence for enhanced (e,e′p) transverse strength of non-single particle origin at high missing energies.

For pm > 200 MeV the cross section is almost constant, (e,e′pp) and (e,e′pn) contributing by about one half of the measured cross section. Besides testing the limits of the single-particle model in one-nucleon knockout, experiments are also proposed to directly observe two nucleons ejected in coincidence with the scattered electron.

accepted.question_text: Which kinematic conditions and final-state selections make exclusive two-nucleon knockout reactions most sensitive to nucleon-nucleon correlations rather than to meson-exchange, isobar, and other two-body current mechanisms? This remains open because the triple-coincidence cross section does not factorize in terms of the two-hole spectral density even without final-state interactions, so extracting correlation information requires identifying observables where correlation effects dominate the competing current contributions.

evidence.quote: Even without FSI the two-hole spectral density is not factorized in the triple coincidence cross section. This makes a difficult task to extract information on correlations from data, and models are required to investigate suitable kinematic conditions where the cross section is particularly sensitive to correlations.

In contrast, (e,e′pp) reactions, where two-body currents play a minor role, are better suited to look for correlations, and resolution of discrete final states has been shown to provide an interesting tool to discriminate between contributions of different mechanisms responsible for two-nucleon emission.

accepted.question_text: Can precise exclusive 16O(e,e′pp) measurements to selected 14C final states, especially transitions dominated by knockout of a relative 1S0 proton pair, be used to determine short-range correlation functions tightly enough to constrain the off-shell behavior of the nucleon-nucleon potential? The unresolved issue is whether sufficiently accurate data in correlation-favored kinematics can distinguish among competing correlation models through their different predictions for these state-resolved cross sections.

evidence.quote: Such transitions are therefore most sensitive to short-range correlations.

As the calculations give significantly different results for different correlation functions, precise data could give important constraint when modelling the off-shell behavior of the nucleon-nucleon potential.
The data are still preliminary and require further analysis before a fully reliable comparison with calculations can be done.

accepted.question_text: How can the two-hole spectral density for proton-neutron knockout be determined accurately enough to disentangle tensor-correlation effects from the large and complicated contributions of meson-exchange and other two-body currents in exclusive (e,e′pn) reactions? In superparallel kinematics the predicted (e,e′pn) cross sections are strongly enhanced, but the open problem is to separate how much of that enhancement comes from tensor correlations and how much comes from two-body current mechanisms.

evidence.quote: Tensor correlations are expected to play a major role in (e,e′pn) reactions where, however, the proton-neutron pair is ejected by a much more complicated mechanism involving two-body currents.
This enhancement is partly due to meson-exchange currents and partly to tensor correlations.
An accurate determination of the two-hole spectral density is thus most desirable in order to disentangle the effects of two-body currents from those of nuclear correlations.

accepted.question_text: Can recoil-polarization measurements in exclusive (e,e′pp) and (e,e′pn) reactions, combined with resolution of specific residual-nucleus final states, provide a practical way to separate correlation-driven knockout from processes generated by two-body currents and thereby determine the full scattering amplitudes more completely? The open problem is whether polarization observables add enough independent information to cleanly decompose the competing reaction mechanisms in two-nucleon emission.

evidence.quote: Experimentally, additional and precise information will come from measurement of the recoil polarization of the ejected proton in either (e,e′pp) or (e,e′pn).
Resolving different final states is a precise filter to disentangle and separately investigate the different processes due to correlations and/or two-body currents.
Ultimately, a complete determination of the scattering amplitudes is only possible with polarization measurements.
